name: Facial nerve rehab / neurectomy

lead: Facial nerve paralysis, most often from Bell's palsy, leaves one side of the face weak and visibly asymmetric. Rehabilitation and surgery aim to restore movement so the face is more balanced at rest and in motion.

Drugs reduce nerve inflammation, rehabilitation techniques aim to improve movement, and surgical options include nerve repair, grafting, nerve transfers and muscle transfers. Neurectomy means cutting selected nerve branches. About 71% of Bell's palsy patients are reported to recover fully, and several rehabilitation trials are registered. This is an established clinical field for paralysis, not a studied route for typical faces.

paras: Care usually starts with a diagnosis, then corticosteroids and therapy with exercises, with surgery considered for longer-lasting or severe cases. It is managed by clinicians such as neurologists, therapists and facial plastic surgeons.
Surgical options carry the usual operative risks. Outcomes of neurectomy were not described in the sources reviewed, and paralysis has many causes that need evaluation.

chain: More balanced face at rest and in motion
angle.text: This is the medical route to a more symmetrical face when facial nerve paralysis has caused droop or uneven movement, using therapy, nerve repair, grafting or muscle transfers to restore movement. It is an established clinical field for paralysis patients.

lead: Facial nerve rehabilitation and neurectomy are medical and surgical approaches to facial asymmetry caused by weakness or abnormal movement of the facial (seventh cranial) nerve. Rehabilitation covers therapy and exercise techniques, drugs given early in the course of a palsy, and procedures such as nerve repair, grafting, nerve transfers and muscle transfers; neurectomy means cutting or removing part of a nerve.[1]

They help someone look better by restoring balance to a face that has dropped, stiffened or moves unevenly after paralysis. When a facial nerve is affected, the smile may pull to one side, the brow may sag, the eye may not close fully and muscles on the unaffected side can look overactive by comparison. Treatment aims to recover movement, reduce abnormal movement, and, where function does not return, rebuild or stand in for it so the face looks more symmetrical at rest and in expression.[1][2]

Facial paralysis has many causes. Bell's palsy is the most common cause of acute onset, and others include Lyme disease and Ramsay Hunt syndrome, trauma, tumours, stroke and congenital conditions.[1] About 71 percent of people with Bell's palsy are reported to recover fully.[1] In looksmaxxing discussion the topic appears as a treatment for paralysis-induced asymmetry rather than as an enhancement for typical faces.

Treatment is multidisciplinary. Acute care for Bell's palsy centres on corticosteroids and eye protection; recovery afterwards can involve facial therapy (movement retraining), botulinum toxin to quiet overactive muscles, selective nerve division (neurolysis or neurectomy) with or without muscle trimming (myectomy), and, when function does not return, nerve transfers and muscle transfers that restore a smile [1][3][4][5][6].

paras: Bell's palsy, of unknown cause but associated with herpes simplex infection, is the most common cause of acute facial paralysis and accounts for about 70 percent of one-sided cases. Other causes include Lyme disease, reactivation of varicella zoster virus (Ramsay Hunt syndrome), middle ear infection, temporal bone fractures, acoustic neuromas and parotid tumours, diabetes, Guillain-Barre syndrome, and Moebius syndrome, which is present at birth.[1]

Wikipedia reports that Lyme disease accounts for about 25 percent of cases in areas where it is common, and that temporal bone fractures are the most common traumatic cause, with transverse fractures carrying a 40 to 50 percent likelihood of paralysis.[1] Stroke produces a central facial palsy that typically spares the forehead, which is how clinicians tell it apart from a nerve (peripheral) palsy.[1]

Weakness is usually one-sided and may develop over several hours to about 72 hours, sometimes preceded by ear pain. Other features can include loss of taste, sensitivity to sound and reduced tears or saliva.[1] Bell's palsy is a diagnosis of exclusion: clinicians check which movements are affected, look for forehead sparing, and use imaging or blood tests when trauma, tumour or Lyme disease are suspected.[1]

The face looks asymmetric after a palsy for several different reasons, and each has a different treatment. Weakness drops the brow, mouth corner and cheek on one side. Incomplete eye closure changes the look of the eyelids and needs protection. After partial recovery, tight, overactive muscles on the affected side can pull the face into an unbalanced expression at rest, and linked movements can narrow the eye when the person smiles [3][4].

Facial Palsy UK describes synkinesis as common in people recovering from long-lasting palsy: regrowing nerve fibres send signals to the wrong muscles, so movements become linked, and muscles on the affected side may be tight rather than weak, causing stiffness, pain or uneven expression [4]. Treatment aims to restore balance by relaxing what is overactive, retraining the brain's muscle recruitment, and reconstructing what has been lost.

For Bell's palsy, corticosteroids are standard, with antivirals added in severe cases, together with eye protection using artificial tears, ointment and taping during sleep [1]. Corticosteroids begun within three days of onset are reported to improve the chance of recovery, by about 14 percent according to Wikipedia's summary of the evidence [1]. A 2015 Cochrane review found no added benefit from antivirals over steroids in mild to moderate disease.

A 2014 Canadian guideline in CMAJ (de Almeida and colleagues, for the Bell Palsy Working Group) strongly recommended corticosteroids corticosteroids for all patients unless contraindicated, advised against antivirals alone, suggested exercise physiotherapy for persistent weakness (weak recommendation, very low confidence), suggested against electrostimulation, recommended routine eye protection, and reserved surgical decompression for select patients [7].

Facial Palsy UK describes movement retraining as the main treatment for synkinesis. A specialist therapist, often a speech and language therapist or physiotherapist, helps the person learn which muscles should work for a given movement, which extra muscles are activating, and how to recruit the right muscles at the right effort, usually with a personalised home programme; some therapists use surface EMG biofeedback [4]. The charity advises that generic facial-strengthening exercises and chewing gum can make synkinesis worse, and reports that with ongoing practice most people reach roughly 70 to 90 percent of previous function [4].

Wikipedia's synkinesis article describes retraining, biofeedback and mime therapy; it reports one study with a 60 to 70 percent average decrease in synkinesis after seven months and says biofeedback works better for prevention when started soon after injury [3]. Registered trials examine Kabat rehabilitation, neural mobilisation, kinesiology taping, photobiomodulation and electrical stimulation in Bell's palsy [8][9][10][11]. Wikipedia notes there is no high-quality evidence for electrical stimulation.

Botulinum toxin injections calm overactive muscles and help rebalance movement; Facial Palsy UK says they work best alongside retraining [4]. Wikipedia's Bell's palsy article describes botulinum toxin as increasingly supported for reducing synkinesis and facial asymmetry. The treatment effect wears off and injections are repeated, with the Wikipedia synkinesis article citing an interval of about three months [3]. In a Modena protocol, injections also targeted selected muscles on the healthy side to improve symmetry [5].

Selective neurolysis, also called neurectomy, permanently divides chosen branches of the facial nerve, and may be combined with myectomy, removal of part of a facial muscle. Facial Palsy UK says surgeons use a nerve stimulator to identify which branch supplies the problem muscle [6]. The operation is usually offered for lower-face synkinesis with lower-lip asymmetry, after extensive therapy and several botulinum toxin sessions have not given enough lasting benefit [6].

In lower-face synkinesis, the neck and lower-lip depressor muscles pull downward against the muscles that lift the mouth. Dividing the nerve to the platysma or the lip depressor frees the smile muscles to act with less opposition, aiming for an easier smile and less tightness; the charity describes the surgery as aimed at comfort and coordination and notes it may reduce some movement when smiling [6]. The procedure is usually under general anaesthetic through an incision in front of the ear, takes about three hours, and is followed by facial therapy beginning two to four weeks later, since surgery alone does not improve expression [6]. Listed risks include damage to nearby structures, under- or over-correction, loss of facial function, infection and scarring; the intended effect is lasting, though long-term evidence is limited [6]. Wikipedia reports that selective myectomy gives more durable relief with a low recurrence rate, whereas neurolysis alone may help only temporarily [3].

Surgical options described by Wikipedia include end-to-end nerve repair after tumour removal, cross-facial nerve grafting, nerve transfers, free muscle transfer and static procedures that restore symmetry when function does not return [1]. A plastic-surgery overview describes the dynamic options in more detail. Cross-facial nerve grafts bring input from the healthy side, so the paralysed side can move spontaneously in step with the unaffected one, but they depend on muscles still being viable; masseteric nerve transfer uses the chewing muscle's nerve to power a smile that usually requires a bite-like effort; the gracilis free muscle transfer, often two-stage with a cross-face graft first, is used when facial muscles will not recover; and temporalis transfer moves a regional muscle to the eye or mouth corner [12]. The overview notes that transposed trigeminal-innervated muscles typically need a clenching manoeuvre rather than producing a spontaneous smile, and that about half of muscle power is typically lost after gracilis transfer [12].

Facial plastic procedures can complement these operations; a registered trial will compare staged deep-plane facelift as an adjunct to reanimation with reanimation alone [13]. Anatomical work on the superficial musculo-aponeurotic system (SMAS), described in 1976 by Mitz and Peyronie, noted its relevance to corrective surgery for facial palsy [2].

After recovery, regenerating nerve fibres can misdirect, so closing the eye may lift the corner of the mouth; Wikipedia reports ongoing problems in about 9 percent of people with Bell's palsy, and other complications include tearing while eating and spasm. Wikipedia's synkinesis article lists three proposed mechanisms: aberrant regeneration, ephaptic cross-talk between poorly insulated nerves, and nuclear hyperexcitability, which most researchers now consider to act together [3].

The Persian physician al-Razi (865 to 925) gave the first known description of facial palsy, and the Scottish neurophysiologist Sir Charles Bell (1774 to 1842) described the facial nerve's role, presenting his work to the Royal Society on 12 July 1821; the condition bears his name.

Most people with Bell's palsy begin to recover within three weeks even without treatment; a 1982 study of 1,011 patients reported early recovery in 85 percent and complete recovery in 71 percent after at least a year. Children under 10 tend to fare better and people over 61 worse. In a study of 30 people with stroke-related paralysis, about two-thirds had full recovery or mild paralysis at six months.[1]

Facial palsy appears in appearance forums mainly as a medical cause of asymmetry. Posts in general fitness and bodybuilding forums discuss Bell's palsy as a personal health event [14]. Patient organisations such as Facial Palsy UK provide guides on synkinesis, surgery and therapy [4][6]. The topic is distinct from non-medical practices aimed at changing a typical face; neurectomy here refers to the selective nerve division used for synkinesis.

A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicentre trial studied prednisolone and valaciclovir in Bell's palsy [15]. A retrospective study at the University Hospital of Modena (2020 to 2023) of 126 patients treated with botulinum toxin A and neuromuscular retraining reported a rise in mean Sunnybrook score from 67.47 to 76.09 after the first injection cycle, and a 11.76-point mean gain after a second cycle in 87 patients; the authors note it had no control group [5].

Several trials of rehabilitation and physical therapies are registered, including Kabat rehabilitation versus conventional physical therapy (n=36) [8], Kabat versus neural mobilisation (completed, n=28) [11], photobiomodulation for idiopathic facial paralysis (completed, n=96) [9], and photobiomodulation with electrical stimulation (not yet recruiting) [10]. A registered trial of deep-plane facelift as a staged adjunct to facial reanimation is also listed [13]. Published outcomes for these registrations have not been reported.

lore.intro: Facial palsy treatment is discussed mainly by patients, therapists and surgeons, and in general health forums, where people compare retraining, botulinum toxin and surgery [4][6][14].

claims.claim: Retraining can restore a more balanced face after palsy.
Botulinum toxin evens out an overactive side.
Selective neurectomy can give a lasting smile improvement in lower-face synkinesis.
Early steroids give the best chance of full recovery in Bell's palsy.
Strengthening exercises will help a weak face.
A transferred muscle can give a natural, spontaneous smile.
